texts.A_interpret:
The global design-by-treatment test rejected the hypothesis of no inconsistency (p = 0.041). Under a fixed-effect model this can reflect unmodelled between-study heterogeneity as well as disagreement between direct and indirect evidence, so read it alongside the random-effects results. Examine the node-split results, the designs involved and study characteristics before relying on network estimates.
4 of 8 node-split comparisons had p < 0.05. These p-values are unadjusted: if there were no inconsistency, about 0.4 of 8 would be expected to reach p < 0.05 by chance, and the splits are correlated (several re-test the same loops). Treat isolated flags as hypothesis-generating, and look at the size of each direct–indirect difference, not only its p-value.
Fixed-effect weights ignore between-study heterogeneity; when heterogeneity is present this inflates Q and makes node-split p-values too small. Compare with the random-effects results.
The comparison of fixed-effect and random-effects results below is a sensitivity analysis: prespecify the primary model rather than choosing it from these results.
Inconsistency tests do not check transitivity (whether effect modifiers are balanced across comparisons). Only independent two-arm studies are supported; multi-arm studies would need their within-study correlation, and excluding them changes the network.

texts.F_methods:
Methods. Inconsistency in the network of 29 independent two-arm studies and 6 treatments was assessed with node-splitting (Dias et al. 2010), computed by back-calculation (König et al. 2013), for every comparison with both direct evidence and an indirect path, and with the global design-by-treatment interaction test (Higgins et al. 2012), using a fixed-effect (common τ² = 0) model. Node-split p-values were not adjusted for multiplicity. Sensitivity of the inconsistency conclusions was assessed by removing each study in turn, and all analyses were repeated under fixed-effect, DerSimonian-Laird and Paule-Mandel models. Analyses used the allmeta nma-inconsistency browser tool, whose node-split, design-by-treatment and leave-one-out results are validated against R netmeta 3.7-0 netsplit() and decomp.design() (relative tolerance 1e-9, 1e-6 for Paule-Mandel; p-values 1e-9 absolute).

Results. The global design-by-treatment test gave Q = 9.99 on 4 df (p = 0.041); 4 of 8 node-split comparisons had p < 0.05 (Fluticasone+Salmeterol vs Tiotropium, p = 0.028; Formoterol vs Placebo, p = 0.043; Formoterol vs Tiotropium, p = 0.043; Placebo vs Tiotropium, p = 0.010). The global test result is fragile: p crosses 0.05 (full data p = 0.041) after removing Mahler 1999, Casaburi 2002, Rossi 2002, Niewoehner 2005, vanNoord 2005, Kardos 2007, Wedzicha 2008 (global p ranged from 0.019 to 0.159 across single-study removals). At least one node-split p-value crosses 0.05 after removing 5 of the 29 studies: Rossi 2002, Niewoehner 2005, Barnes 2006, Kardos 2007, Wedzicha 2008. With full-data p close to 0.05 (Formoterol vs Placebo, p = 0.043; Formoterol vs Tiotropium, p = 0.043), such crossings are expected and do not by themselves identify influential studies. Global design-by-treatment p was 0.041 with fixed-effect, 0.146 with DerSimonian-Laird (τ² = 0.0147) and 0.169 with Paule-Mandel (τ² = 0.0182) weights. The models fall on different sides of 0.05; with τ² > 0 the fixed-effect result is sensitive to unmodelled heterogeneity. 4 of 8 node-split p-values fall on different sides of 0.05 depending on the model.

cmpSummary: Global design-by-treatment p was 0.041 with fixed-effect, 0.146 with DerSimonian-Laird (τ² = 0.0147) and 0.169 with Paule-Mandel (τ² = 0.0182) weights. The models fall on different sides of 0.05; with τ² > 0 the fixed-effect result is sensitive to unmodelled heterogeneity. 4 of 8 node-split p-values fall on different sides of 0.05 depending on the model.
